conservation.notes: Downgraded to Near Threatened in 2004 after an apparent 65.5% decline over 40 years, then returned to Least Concern in 2018. Still has a threatened status in Canada and several US states, and has declined more than 1.5% a year from 1966 to 2015 in the Mississippi and Ohio river valleys.

human_tolerance.notes: Historically a common bird of the heavily altered east-central United States, and it will nest in utility poles and fence posts as readily as in dead trees, but it needs standing dead wood in the wider neighbourhood and has lost ground to starlings for cavity sites.

phases.name: territorial
phases.note: A mature male establishes a territory and begins calling and drumming to attract a mate; on an established territory both parents become very territorial and will destroy the nests and eggs of other birds inside it.

phases.name: nesting
phases.note: The female chooses the cavity site by tapping on it, then both parents drill it out if it is not already a cavity, the male doing most of the work. Sites are mostly in dead trees or utility poles 2.45 to 24.5 m above the ground. In early May she lays four to seven white eggs, incubated about two weeks, the female by day and the male at night.

phases.name: young
phases.note: Both parents care for the young, which stay in the cavity until they fledge, usually 27 to 31 days after hatching.

phases.name: caching
phases.note: Food is stuffed into tree cavities, crevices and under bark, which keeps the bird fed through the winter; this is a habit shared with only three other woodpeckers.

vocalizations.description: A 'tchur-tchur' call, given by both sexes to advertise and defend a territory and to attract a mate, and heard through the breeding season. The behaviour program has no separate alarm slot for this species, so its alarm step plays this documented call rather than an invented one.

Drumming on its territory, the mechanical counterpart of the call: the bird hammers a dead branch, stump or resonant tree, which is how a territory is announced at a distance. No duration band is claimed because the cited article gives none.

external.note: GBIF usageKey 2478130 and family Picidae from the GBIF Backbone record for the accepted name; iNaturalist taxon id 18204 from the iNaturalist taxa API; ITIS TSN 178186 from the ITISWebService scientific-name search, which returns Melanerpes erythrocephalus (Linnaeus, 1758) as an exact match; Wikidata Q578174 from a Wikidata entity search for the scientific name.

common_names.note: Catesby 'used the English name "The Red-headed Wood-pecker"' in 1729-1732.

conservation.note: IUCN category from Wikidata P141, which points at the IUCN 'Least Concern' item; the history and the Ohio-valley decline come from the article's status section, which records the 2004 downlisting to Near Threatened and the 2018 return to Least Concern.

range.note: Country list derived from 'historically a common species in southern Canada and the east-central United States' plus the Florida and Wisconsin records in the same article.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: A woodpecker grips trunks and branches to climb, works along limbs and bark, and flies and glides between trees; the article's own actions are drilling, hammering, drumming and flying between dead trees and poles.

traits.nest_type.note: 'If the chosen site does not already have a nesting cavity, then both parents will drill out the nesting cavity', in dead trees or utility poles: a cavity nest.

traits.mass_kg.note: 'They weigh from 56 to 97 g (2.0 to 3.4 oz), with an average of 76 g (2.7 oz)'; the stated average is used directly.

traits.length_m.note: Midpoint of 'Both sexes measure from 19 to 25 cm'.

traits.wingspan_m.note: 'with a wingspan of 42.5 cm (16.7 in)', used directly.

traits.lifespan_y.note: 'The maximum longevity in the wild is 9.9 years', used directly.

traits.diet.note: 'The red-headed woodpecker is omnivorous, eating insects, seeds, fruits, berries, nuts, and occasionally small rodents - even the eggs of other birds. About two-thirds of its diet consists of plants.' fruit 0.35 and seed 0.30 make 0.65, i.e. the stated two-thirds of plants; invertebrate 0.30 covers the insects and other invertebrates gleaned from bark, and vertebrate 0.05 covers the rodents and eggs.

traits.social.note: A territorial pair that drills one cavity and cares for the brood together; the article describes no flocking, so the group size stops at 2.

traits.defense.note: 'When in an established territory, the parents become very territorial. They have been known to destroy nests and eggs of other birds in their territory.' That is active attack on an intruder, not withdrawal, so Mob.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement at 0.4: it nests in utility poles and fence posts and was historically common in altered country, so it is comfortable near people, but it is a bird of open woodland edges and needs dead wood, so it does not tolerate a bare built-up lot.

habitat.use.note: 'Factors attributed to the red-headed woodpecker's decline include loss of overall habitat and, within habitats, loss of standing dead wood required for nest sites'; the bird works bark and trunks and flies between trees, so arboreal takes 0.85 and the brief ground foraging 0.15.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: It holds and drills one cavity, which it also uses as a winter roost, so the site it depends on is a cavity.

habitat.resources.note: The omnivore list for the feeding tags, the nest-hole and winter-cavity sentences for `cavity`, and the drumming and territory statements for `perch`. The bird's attacks on the nests and eggs of other birds are not a feeding resource, so they are carried by traits.defense rather than by a resource tag.

habitat.requires.note: 'loss of standing dead wood required for nest sites' and 'competition for nesting cavities with the invasive European starling': the bird needs an uncontested cavity within its territory. 500 m is an authored radius for a cavity in a scene; the article states no distance.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Nest sites 'could be a natural cavity, the wintering cavity used by the male, a cavity used the season before, a fence post, utility poles, or a dead tree', in country the article calls heavily altered; the numeric tolerances are authored around that.

seasonal.strategy.note: Resident across its historic southern Canadian and east-central US range, with the article noting that birds seen in northern Wisconsin 'typically don't overwinter': Ohio birds are largely resident, so PartialMigration.

seasonal.winter_fraction.note: Judgement at 0.7, from the article's southern-Canada and east-central-US range against the note that northern Wisconsin birds do not overwinter. The article gives no proportion.

seasonal.phases.note: The territorial call and drum, the female's cavity choice and the parents' drilling, the early-May laying of four to seven eggs with about two weeks of incubation split between the parents by day and night, the 27-to-31-day nestling period and the autumn food caching all come from the article; the month boundaries are judgements.

seasonal.life_stages.note: 'The young will stay in the nest until they are old enough to fledge, which is usually after 27 to 31 days'; duration_days is the upper end of that window and scale 0.9 is a judgement for the nestling.

vocalizations.call.note: 'This species gives a tchur-tchur call or a drum on its territory' and 'a mature male ... will establish a territory and begin calling and drumming to attract a mate.' The behaviour program needs both a song and an alarm call id, and the article documents only this one call, so both point at it rather than at an invented alarm; no openly licensed recording is cited, so no `recordings` entry is claimed.

vocalizations.drum.note: 'a drum on its territory' is the article's own wording; the season and the loudness are the field's judgement, and no recording is cited.

look.note: 'Red-headed woodpeckers are entirely crimson above their shoulders', with a black back, white underparts and large white patches on the wings and rump, and a dark bill. The head is coloured from `markings`, the white wing panels and rump from `accent`, and the proportions are authored from the 19-25 cm length and the stated 42.5 cm wingspan.

behavior.note: bt-perching-songbird-v1 is the shared program for a bird that holds a defended territory, announces it vocally, roosts in a cavity, drills and uses a nest and takes food near a perch; it is the closest of the four shared programs for a woodpecker. food_tag is `invertebrate`, the bark-and-trunk foraging the bird is built for, and flee_m is raised to 15 m because the bird holds a large territory instead of withdrawing from a walker. The program's ground foraging step is an approximation: this bird feeds on bark and in the canopy, not on the ground.
